summary: Defines the procedures and extensions to RSVP-TE needed to support unnumbered links in MPLS traffic engineering. The signaling at the time did not support links that have no IP address of their own, which this document addresses.

eli5.summary: Some network links do not have their own address, like a road with no name. This note shows how to set up paths over such links anyway.

questions: mpls te links without ip addresses
what is an unnumbered link in mpls
how does rsvp-te signal unnumbered links
what is the lsp tunnel interface id object
subtitle: How RSVP-TE names point-to-point links that have no IP address, so MPLS traffic-engineered paths can cross them.

tldr.problem: MPLS traffic engineering signalling had no way to name an unnumbered link (one without an IP address) in its Explicit Route and Record Route Objects.
tldr.mechanism: Each end of an unnumbered link assigns it a non-zero 32-bit identifier. A new Unnumbered Interface ID subobject (type 4, length 12) pairs a Router ID with that identifier in the ERO and RRO, and a new LSP_TUNNEL_INTERFACE_ID object handles Forwarding Adjacencies.
tldr.outcome: RSVP-TE signalling can now route and record paths over unnumbered links. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and was later updated by RFC 6107.

today: RFC 3477 is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 6107; it has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: The Unnumbered Link Problem
sections.content:
Supporting MPLS traffic engineering (MPLS TE) over unnumbered links, meaning links that do not have IP addresses, takes two things. First, the routing protocols (IS-IS or OSPF) must carry TE information about such links. Second, the signalling must be able to name them. The RFC covers only the second part; the first is left to separate GMPLS extensions for IS-IS and OSPF.

The gap is specific. The signalling in use at the time had no way to indicate an unnumbered link in its Explicit Route Object (ERO) or Record Route Object (RRO), because those objects identified hops by IP address. RFC 3477 adds simple procedures and extensions so that RSVP-TE signalling, as described in RFC 3473, works with unnumbered links.
sections.eli5: A route that lists every stop by street address breaks when one road has no address. This note adds a new way to name those roads.

sections.title: Link Identifiers and Router IDs
sections.content:
An unnumbered link has to be a point-to-point link. The router at each end (an LSR) assigns the link an identifier: a non-zero 32-bit number that is unique within the scope of the LSR that assigns it. If IS-IS or OSPF and RSVP both run on the LSR, their modules must agree on the identifiers.

There is no relationship between the identifier one end picks and the one the other end picks. From LSR A's view, the number A assigned is the link local identifier and the number B assigned is the link remote identifier; B sees the reverse. The two ends must learn each other's numbers. The RFC lists several ways to do that: configuration, a protocol such as LMP, RSVP or CR-LDP (especially for a Forwarding Adjacency), or IS-IS and OSPF extensions.

The RFC also uses the term Router ID for a stable IP address of an LSR that is always reachable while the LSR has any connectivity, typically a loopback address. When OSPF or IS-IS carries TE information, it is RECOMMENDED that the Router ID be the OSPF TE "Router Address" or the IS-IS "Traffic Engineering Router ID". All of this also applies to unnumbered component links of a bundled link.
sections.eli5: Each end of the path picks its own number for it, like two kids who each give the same tree house a different nickname. They swap nicknames so they can talk about it.

sections.title: Unnumbered Forwarding Adjacencies
sections.content:
A Forwarding Adjacency is an LSP that is advertised in IS-IS or OSPF as if it were a link, or that is used as a component link of a bundled link. When one is unnumbered, the head-end LSR MUST allocate an identifier for it, just as for any unnumbered link. The Path message that sets up the LSP MUST carry the LSP_TUNNEL_INTERFACE_ID object, with the head end's Router ID and the identifier it allocated.

The tail end answers in kind. If the Path message carries that object, the tail-end LSR MUST allocate an identifier too, and the Resv message MUST carry an LSP_TUNNEL_INTERFACE_ID object with the tail end's Router ID and its identifier.

When the ERO and IF_ID RSVP_HOP objects are processed, the Forwarding Adjacency is treated like an ordinary unnumbered link. The originating LSR uses its own allocated value as the local identifier and the Interface ID from the Reverse Interface ID object as the remote one. The tail end does the opposite, taking the remote value from the Forward Interface ID object.
sections.eli5: When a whole tunnel is treated as one big road, both ends of the tunnel give it a number and tell each other. After that it acts like any other numbered-by-nickname road.

sections.title: The New Object and Subobjects
sections.content:
The LSP_TUNNEL_INTERFACE_ID object has class number 193, C-Type 1 and length 12. It holds the LSR's Router ID and a 32-bit Interface ID. In a Path message it is called the Forward Interface ID; in a Resv message it is the Reverse Interface ID.

For explicit routes, a new ERO subobject, the Unnumbered Interface ID, has type 4 and length 12. Its fields are an L bit, the type, a length, 16 reserved bits that MUST be zero, the Router ID, and the Interface ID assigned to the link by the LSR named by that Router ID.

The RRO has a matching subobject, also type 4 and length 12, to record that the path crossed an unnumbered link. It has a Flags byte instead of the L bit. Flag 0x01 means local protection is available for the link downstream of the node; it can only be set if the Local protection flag was set in the SESSION_ATTRIBUTE object of the corresponding Path message. Flag 0x02 means a local repair mechanism is in use to maintain the tunnel.
sections.eli5: The new labels are like a form with two blanks: the name of the town and the number of the road. A second form records the roads you actually drove.

sections.title: Processing the ERO, IF_ID and RRO
sections.content:
An Unnumbered Interface ID subobject belongs to an abstract node if that node's Router ID equals the subobject's Router ID, and the node has an unnumbered link or Forwarding Adjacency whose local identifier equals the subobject's Interface ID. After that, ERO processing follows the rules in section 4.3.4.1 of RFC 3209. When the chosen outgoing link is unnumbered, the Path message sent to the next hop MUST include the IF_ID RSVP_HOP object, with its IP address field set to the node's Router ID and its Interface ID field set to the link identifier the node assigned.

On the receiving side, an LSR that gets a Path message with the IF_ID RSVP_HOP object and an IF_INDEX TLV looks for a link whose tuple of Router ID and local identifier matches the IP address and Interface ID in the TLV. A match identifies the link for label allocation. If there is none, the LSR SHOULD return an error in the IF_ID ERROR_SPEC object, with Error code 24 and Error value 16.

For the RRO, if the ERO subobject used to pick the next hop is of type Unnumbered Interface ID and an RRO was received (or is desired in the original Path message), an Unnumbered Interface ID RRO subobject MUST be appended before the Path message goes downstream. For any other ERO subobject type, and for label recording, the procedures of RFC 3209 apply.
sections.eli5: Each router checks whether the town and road number in the route match one of its own roads. If they do, it passes the message on and says which road it used. If not, it reports an error.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC treats this as a small extension to RFC 3209 that refines and spells out the use of unnumbered links, so it says it poses no new security concerns. It adds, as an aside, that the extra interface identifier could make an RSVP message harder to spoof.
sections.eli5: This note only adds a new way to name roads, so it does not open any new doors for trouble.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: The document defines a new subobject for the EXPLICIT_ROUTE object and for the ROUTE_RECORD object. Subobject numbers are assigned under the rules in RFC 3209. IANA also needs to assign a class number to the LSP_TUNNEL_INTERFACE_ID object. That number must have the form 11bbbbbb, so that RSVP silently ignores the object if it does not know it, but still forwards it.
sections.eli5: A registry keeper hands out the official numbers. The new object gets a number that old routers will skip over politely and pass along.
